source_batch.unit_label: Module A: International Banking - Correspondent Banking and NRI Accounts

facts.statement: Under Schedule III of the NDI Rules, as amended by the Third Amendment Rules (S.O. 3030(E), 12 June 2026), investment in equity instruments of a listed Indian company on a recognised stock exchange is open to all individual persons resident outside India, where it was previously permitted only to NRIs and OCIs, with enhanced investment limits. Banks may open a repatriable rupee account for the purpose; breaches are reclassified from portfolio to direct investment under the FPI framework. The circular does not state the new limit figures.
facts.locator: Paragraphs 1 to 2 of A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No. 14 dated 15 June 2026; S03 printed p. 80 states the older limits (5% individual, 10% aggregate)

facts.statement: Repatriation basis (Schedule III): payment is by inward remittance through banking channels or out of a repatriable deposit account; the investor designates a repatriable rupee account used only for these investments; sale proceeds (net of taxes) of equity may be remitted abroad or credited to that designated account; sale proceeds of mutual fund units may be remitted outside India or credited to any account under the Deposit Regulations at the NRI/OCI's option.
facts.locator: Section 3.1, Schedule III, parts A and B

facts.statement: Non-repatriation basis (Schedule IV): an NRI or OCI buying equity instruments, units or a contribution to the capital of an LLP pays by inward remittance or out of NRE, FCNR(B) or NRO funds; the sale or maturity proceeds (net of taxes) are credited only to the NRO account, whichever account paid; the amount invested and the capital appreciation cannot be repatriated. The same treatment applies to an investment in a firm or proprietary concern.
facts.locator: Section 3.1, Schedule IV, paragraphs 1 and 2; S03 printed p. 81 agrees on non-repatriable investment

facts.statement: An NRI or OCI may purchase immovable property in India other than agricultural land, a farm house or plantation property; may acquire it as a gift from a relative who is a resident, NRI or OCI, or by inheritance; may sell non-agricultural property to a resident, NRI or OCI; and may sell or gift agricultural land only to a resident. Payment must be through banking channels or out of NRE, FCNR(B) or NRO accounts, not through travellers' cheques or foreign currency notes.
facts.locator: Part II, Q1 and Q2; S03 printed pp. 81-82 agrees in substance

facts.statement: NRIs and PIOs may remit the sale proceeds of immovable property other than agricultural land, a farm house or plantation property if the property was acquired in accordance with the foreign exchange law in force at the time, or the NDI Rules, and the price was paid in foreign exchange received through banking channels or out of FCNR(B) or NRE funds; for residential property, repatriation is restricted to not more than two such properties. Repatriation up to USD 1 million per financial year, along with other assets, is allowed under the Remittance of Assets Regulations, 2016.
facts.locator: Part II, Q7; S03 printed p. 82 agrees on the two-property restriction

facts.statement: Citizens of Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, China, Iran, Nepal, Bhutan, Macau, Hong Kong or the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, irrespective of residential status, cannot acquire or transfer immovable property in India without the prior permission of the Reserve Bank, other than on lease not exceeding five years; the prohibition does not apply to an OCI.
facts.locator: Part II, Q4; S03 printed p. 82 lists ten countries and omits the Democratic People's Republic of Korea

payload.title: Two ways to invest: money that can leave, money that stays
payload.core_explanation_md:
When an NRI invests in India, the first decision is the **route**, because it fixes where the money may go on exit.

**Repatriation route** (Schedule III, listed equity and mutual fund units)
- Pay by inward remittance, or from a **repatriable** deposit account. A designated repatriable rupee account is used only for these investments.
- Sale proceeds (net of taxes) may be **sent abroad** or kept in that designated account. For mutual fund units, the NRI chooses between remitting and any permitted account.

**Non-repatriation route** (Schedule IV: equity, units, LLP capital; also firms and proprietary concerns)
- Pay by remittance, or from an **NRE, FCNR(B) or NRO** account.
- Proceeds go **only to the NRO account**, whichever account paid. The amount invested and the gain **cannot be repatriated**.

Shortcut: *repatriable in, repatriable out; non-repatriable investments always come back to an NRO account.*

payload.title: Shares on the stock exchange: what changed in June 2026
payload.core_explanation_md:
Courseware written before mid-2026 describes the **Portfolio Investment Scheme**: only NRIs and PIOs, through a designated bank branch, up to 5% of a company's paid-up capital each and 10% for all NRIs together.

On **12 June 2026** the Government amended the Non-Debt Instruments Rules (S.O. 3030(E)), and on **15 June 2026** the Reserve Bank gave effect to it in A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No. 14:

- **Who**: every **individual person resident outside India**, not only NRIs and OCIs, may buy and sell shares of listed Indian companies on a recognised stock exchange on a repatriation basis.
- **Limits**: **enhanced** from the old 5% and 10%. The circular itself does not state the new figures.
- **Account**: the bank opens a repatriable rupee account for the investor.
- **Breach of limits**: the holding is reclassified from portfolio investment to direct investment under the framework for foreign portfolio investors.

For the exam, remember the **direction of change** (wider eligibility, higher limits). Do not quote the old 5% and 10% as current.

self_check.prompt_text: A foreign national with no Indian roots lives abroad and wants to buy shares of a listed Indian company on the stock exchange. Before June 2026, could he use the NRI route, and what is the position now?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Before June 2026 the route was only for NRIs and OCIs, so no. Since the June 2026 amendment, any individual resident outside India may use Schedule III, subject to the enhanced limits.

payload.title: Buying and selling property in India as an NRI
payload.core_explanation_md:
What an NRI or OCI may do with immovable property in India:

- **Buy**: residential or commercial property from a resident, NRI or OCI. **Not** agricultural land, a farm house or plantation property.
- **Receive as gift** (not agricultural): from a relative who is a resident, NRI or OCI. **Inherit**: any property, from anyone who acquired it lawfully.
- **Sell or gift**: non-agricultural property to a resident, NRI or OCI; **agricultural land only to a resident**.
- **Pay for it**: through banking channels, or from **NRE, FCNR(B) or NRO** accounts. Not by travellers' cheques or foreign currency notes.

Restricted buyers: citizens of Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, China, Iran, Nepal, Bhutan, Macau, Hong Kong and North Korea need prior RBI permission (other than for a lease of up to five years), but this bar **does not apply to an OCI**.

payload.title: Sending the sale proceeds of a property abroad
payload.core_explanation_md:
Selling the property is easy; sending the money out has conditions. For non-agricultural property sold by an NRI or PIO:

1. The property must have been **acquired lawfully** under the exchange rules then in force.
2. The **price must have been paid in foreign exchange** through banking channels, or from FCNR(B) or NRE funds.
3. For **residential** property, repatriation covers **not more than two properties**.

In addition, repatriation sits within the **USD 1 million per financial year** facility, which covers the person's other eligible assets too.

worked_steps.description: Check how each flat was paid for: foreign exchange through banking channels, or FCNR(B) or NRE funds.

The remaining flat is not excluded from sale, only from repatriation of its proceeds. The proceeds of any repatriated flats also count within USD 1 million per financial year.

unresolved: Government securities, treasury bills, PSU bonds, mutual fund and company fixed-deposit purchases without limit (printed pp. 81-82) are not taught: they were not found in the RBI sources fetched.

The new Schedule III limit figures are not stated by RBI circular 14. Secondary sources (EY, TaxGuru) say the individual limit is below 10% and the aggregate 24%; the Rules text was not retrieved, so no item states these figures and the card tells learners the direction of change only.
The courseware (printed p. 80) gives the older 5% and 10% limits and a Portfolio Investment Scheme description that the June 2026 amendment supersedes.
Courseware printed p. 82 mentions a ten-year lock-in for property bought while resident; the RBI FAQ fetched does not state it, so it is not taught.
Conditions on investing in a firm or proprietary concern (not agricultural, plantation or real estate business) are in the Rules text, not the regulations fetched; not taught.

RBI FAQ Part II Q7(a) says property held under FEMA section 6(5) (owned while resident, or inherited from a resident) cannot have its sale proceeds repatriated without RBI approval, while Q7(b) separately allows up to USD 1 million per year for some of the same persons; the interplay is not clear from the FAQ, so it is not taught.
